title: VideoAnchor: Reinforcing Visual Cues Across Frames
one_liner: A plug-and-play module that anchors a vision-language model's focus to the same objects across video frames by using a mathematical fact: points in a cluster can be written as mixtures of other points in that cluster.
lead: When a vision-language model (a system that looks at images and answers questions about them) watches a video, it should recognize the same objects in each frame. But instead, language words hog all the model's focus (the mechanism that decides which pieces to emphasize), drowning out the visual pieces. VideoAnchor fixes this by using a mathematical fact from clustering: when objects form a tight group, each object can be written as a mixture of the others in that group. It uses this fact to find which visual pieces (small patches of pixels) across frames are likely the same object by measuring how well they blend with each other, then boosts those pieces' importance, without retraining the whole model.

problem.h2: Vision-language models forget visual cues in videos
paras: A vision-language model processes a video by breaking each image into pieces (small patches of pixels). When answering a question, the model uses a focus system (the part that decides which pieces matter most) to weight each piece by importance. The problem: language pieces (the words in the question) dominate, so picture pieces get pushed to the background. Worse, when watching a sequence of frames, the model treats each frame alone. If a box appears in frames 1, 3, and 5, the model might spot it once and forget it the other times.

A beginner might try making the model bigger or retraining on videos. Both are slow and fragile. The deeper problem: the focus weights are driven by language alone, with nothing tying the same picture objects together across frames.

callout.html: Picture pieces fade into the background because language pieces attract all the focus, and there is nothing tying the same picture objects together across frames.

steps.text: For each frame, build a small table showing how similar each picture piece is to every other piece.
Use the similarity pattern to estimate which pieces belong to the same cluster (a group of related objects).
When similar clusters appear in consecutive frames, mark which pieces in the new frame match the old frame's cluster.
Increase the focus weight for pieces that match, so they rise above language noise.
Plug the module in front of the model and run the model on new questions. The model itself stays unchanged.

paras: VideoAnchor modifies one thing: the focus scores (the raw weights before the final step that turns raw scores into percentages adding to 100%) for picture pieces in video frames. It does not retrain the model's numbers, add new numbers, or change how the model is built. It computes a small bonus based on which pieces are similar across frames and adds that bonus to the focus scores, lifting important picture pieces out of the shadow of language.

hidden.h2: Cluster matching strength: the glue holding frames together
hidden.name: How tightly pieces cluster across frames
paras: This is the central quantity the method measures. When objects form a tight group, each object can be written as a blend of the others in that group. For video pieces, this means: if a dog appears in frame 1 and frame 2, the dog pieces in frame 2 should be expressible (writable as a blend) using dog pieces from frame 1. This blend strength is high when the pieces are truly the same object and low when they are unrelated.

VideoAnchor estimates this by building a similarity table (a grid where each cell is a score) and looking for which piece pairs have the highest match score (closeness). A high match score between frame 1's piece and frame 2's piece means they are likely the same picture object.

heat.caption: Darker means pieces are more similar. Marked cells are the dog across frames.

reads.html: Match strength is how much one piece can be built from others. High match means they are the same thing.
Self-expressiveness property: when pieces form a cluster, any piece can be written as a blend of cluster neighbors. A match table detects which piece sets form coherent patterns across time.

mechanism.h2: Why tying frames together fixes the problem
paras: The root cause is that focus is purely local: each frame is scored independently, with no memory of past frames. Language pieces win every time because the model learned from text, so it favors language by default. VideoAnchor breaks this by adding a second scoring channel: cluster match strength, which is mathematical and does not care if a piece is a noun or a number. When the same picture cluster (the dog, the background, a moving hand) appears in the next frame, its pieces get a boost because the match score says they belong to the same cluster as before. This boost is small (0.1 times the match score), so it does not change the model's core learned weightings; but it is consistent and cumulative across frames, so picture pieces with matching neighbors gradually climb above noise. The mechanism is a shortcut: instead of retraining the model to care more about pictures, we add a hint saying this picture piece matches a past picture piece, so focus on it.

stages.s: Frame sequence and picture pieces from all frames
Build similarity table for each frame's pieces
Match high-score pieces across consecutive frames
Add match bonuses to picture piece focus scores
Boosted focus scores; picture pieces now visible to the model

math.equation: B = alpha * SE(P_i, P_j) * M(t_k, t_k+1)
symbols: the focus score increase for piece P_j
a small constant controlling boost strength (e.g., 0.1)
blend strength: how much piece j can be written as a mix of piece i
match score: 1 if piece j in frame k+1 is the same object as i in frame k, else 0

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Piece A (frame 1 dog): blend strength = 0.9, cross-frame match = 1.0, alpha = 0.1
Piece B (frame 1 background): blend strength = 0.3, cross-frame match = 0.0 (no match in frame 2)
Piece A's focus score rises by 0.09 (small but visible), while B stays flat.

math.note: The formula multiplies three numbers: alpha (set to 0.1), blend strength (how well the piece fits its cluster), and frame match (whether the piece is the same object in the next frame).

items.html: If an object moves too fast or rotates sharply between frames, piece similarity drops below the threshold, and the match fails. The dog jumps suddenly; the dog in frame 2 looks too different from frame 1.

items.b: Multiple similar objects trick the anchor.
items.html: If two dogs are in the scene, the cluster match might link the wrong one across frames, pulling focus to the wrong place. Similarity alone does not solve identity.

If the dog is hidden behind a tree in frame 3, the model cannot see the dog pieces in that frame (they are physically absent from the image), so there are no pieces to boost; the anchor fails silently because it only works when a matching piece is visible in both frames.
Slow or moderate motion, distinct objects, and simple scenes are where VideoAnchor works well.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small test: take a 5-frame video of a hand moving slowly across a table, with the same hand visible in frames 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Write a simple question: 'Where is the hand in frame 3?' Without VideoAnchor, the model guesses randomly or defaults to early frames. With the module, it should track the hand and place it in the correct position in frame 3. The metric is spatial accuracy: did the model point to the right region?
demo.closing: The demo must show that the module keeps picture pieces visible across frames, not just in the first frame.
